# Luke 23:1–28: Research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**Gaps in what I found:**
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** On newadvent.org I only reached the Bible text (Knox translation and Vulgate), not a commentary. I found nothing on catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage.
- **Not reached at all:** Methodist sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) and bibleodyssey.org. The Methodist and Lutheran voices below come from older commentaries on StudyLight.
- **NET Bible notes:** The page I read cut off after note 23, so I only have notes for vv. 1–7. Nothing from NET on v. 17 or later.

---

**v. 1**
- Rome did not let the Jewish leaders carry out executions, so they took Jesus to Pilate. Guzik also cites Philo's very harsh description of Pilate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- The Pulpit Commentary says the council's death sentence was illegal by Jewish rules, because a capital verdict could not be given on the day of the trial. It also gives Pilate's background (appointed through Sejanus, governed for ten years, removed in disgrace). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- MacArthur (Baptist) says all these characters thought they could decide what happened to Jesus, but in reality, the destiny of Jesus had been determined by God. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-278/jesus-accused-before-pilate-part-1

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the leaders knew Pilate would not care about a charge of blasphemy, so they brought three false political charges: being a revolutionary, telling people not to pay taxes, and claiming to be a king against Caesar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- NET note: the tax charge was a lie (it points back to Luke 20:20–26). The second and third charges directly challenged Roman authority, so Pilate had to act. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23
- MacArthur: They can't go to Pilate and say, "Kill Him because of blasphemy," that's not a civil crime. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-278/jesus-accused-before-pilate-part-1

**v. 3**
- NET: Pilate cared only about the king charge because it implied rebellion against Rome. Jesus' answer, "You say so," is "somewhat enigmatic," like His answer to the council in 22:70. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23
- Pulpit: Pilate ignored the first two charges as baseless. Luke gives only a short summary; John 18:33–38 gives the fuller conversation, which John probably witnessed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Guzik: Jesus looked beaten rather than royal, so Pilate probably asked the question with sarcasm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 4**
- NET: this is the first of several statements in Luke 23 that Jesus is innocent, or attempts to release Him (vv. 13–16, 20, 22). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23
- F.B. Meyer sees Jesus here as God's Passover Lamb, searched to discover if there were spot, or blemish. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/luke-23.html

**v. 5**
- Utley (bible.org): the accusers added "starting from Galilee" to make Jesus look more like a traitor. Galilee was a hotbed of seditious activity. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-23
- NET: repeating the charge of stirring up rebellion put pressure on Pilate, who could otherwise be accused of ignoring a political threat. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23

**vv. 6–7: commentators differ on why Pilate sent Jesus to Herod**
- **To get rid of the case.** NET says Pilate wanted to rid himself of the problem. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23 Matthew Henry says Pilate was already sick of the cause, and desirous to rid his hands of it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_023.cfm The Pulpit Commentary says he feared being reported to Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- **To get advice.** Constable disagrees: Pilate meant to secure Herod's counsel in Jesus' case, not to pass off his responsibility. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-23.html
- **To pay Herod a courtesy.** Guzik quotes Clarke (Methodist), who thinks Pilate was glad of the chance to show Herod some respect. Guzik also notes that "sent" was a technical word for transferring a prisoner between authorities. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- **Herod's presence in Jerusalem.** NET: Herod had probably come for the feast; Josephus records him at a feast in Jerusalem. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23

**v. 8**
- Guzik: Herod only wanted to be entertained. He had once listened to John the Baptist but had become dead to conscience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- The Pulpit Commentary quotes Godet: to Herod, Jesus was like a juggler to a bored court, a mere curiosity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Barclay: Herod regarded Jesus as a joke. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/luke-23.html

**v. 9**
- Pett links Jesus' silence to Isaiah 53:7 (the sheep silent before its shearers). He says Jesus had already convinced Pilate and saw no point in putting on a show. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-23.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: the Lord who answered blind beggars stays silent before a prince who is only curious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 10**
- Pett: this verse sits at the centre of the passage's structure. It highlights the chief priests and scribes as the main culprits, though their plan only worked because those responsible for justice failed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-23.html

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: Herod treated Jesus as a contemptible religious enthusiast, not a criminal. The robe was probably a bright white festal mantle of the kind kings and nobles wore. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- R.M. Edgar reads the white robe as Herod's own witness that Jesus was innocent, the second such testimony. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Matthew Henry: Herod knew more about Christ than Pilate did and was more abusive, for knowledge without grace does but make men the more ingeniously wicked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_023.cfm

**v. 12: commentators differ on what joined Herod and Pilate**
- **Shared hostility to Christ.** The Geneva Study Bible notes: The hatred of godliness binds the wicked together. The Pulpit Commentary points to Acts 4:27. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/23-12.htm
- **Not hatred.** Barnes (Presbyterian) disagrees: Pilate wanted to release Jesus, and both men treated Him as a joke rather than an enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/23-12.htm
- **The cause of the earlier quarrel.** Ellicott says the cause is unknown; Herod "passes no formal sentence." https://biblehub.com/luke/23-12.htm Others guess it was the killing of Galileans in Luke 13:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/23-12.htm
- **A different emphasis.** Pett reads the friendship as the real "miracle" Herod got that day, a sign of Jesus as Prince of Peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-23.html

**vv. 13–15**
- Constable: Pilate used standard legal language. Herod, as a Semitic ruler, was an authority the crowd may have respected more than Pilate, and the two men agreed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-23.html
- Pett: Pilate should simply have released Jesus. His delay encouraged the accusers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-23.html

**v. 16**
- The commentators agree this was unjust:
  - Pulpit: singularly unjust and cruel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
  - Kretzmann (Lutheran) calls it Pilate's first grievous public mistake. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/luke-23.html
  - Guzik describes how brutal Roman scourging was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**v. 17 (textual question)**
- Pulpit: The more ancient authorities omit this verse. It was probably a marginal note borrowed from Matthew 27:15 or Mark 15:6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Guzik still comments on it: Pilate hoped the Passover release custom would let Jesus escape. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/

**vv. 18–19**
- Utley: "Away with" here carries the sense "take away and kill." https://bible.org/export/html/21320 (I found this page only as a search result; the URL should probably read bible.org/book/export/html/21320.)
- Constable: Barabbas was the opposite of Jesus. He was guilty of the very rebellion Jesus was cleared of, and Jesus restored life where Barabbas took it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-23.html
- Pulpit: "Barabbas" means "son of a (famous) father." Origen knew a reading "Jesus Barabbas," but the Pulpit says it is not in the more trustworthy manuscripts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Barabbas as a picture of substitution: Bell says Jesus took his place (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/luke-23.html), and Guzik says much the same (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/).

**vv. 20–23**
- Barclay counts four attempts by Pilate to avoid condemning Jesus and concludes he was coerced. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/luke-23.html
- Kretzmann: Pilate had lost control; reasoning with the mob was like trying to stop a tornado. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/luke-23.html
- Guzik thinks the shouting crowd was mostly Jerusalem locals, not the Galilean pilgrims of Palm Sunday. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- Matthew Henry: Pilate should have done justice without asking leave of them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-20.html

**v. 24**
- Pulpit: Pilate's selfish fears for himself overpowered all sense of reverence, awe, and justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-23.html
- Constable cites a writer who says Pilate wanted to be popular rather than right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-23.html

**v. 25**
- Guzik: in a deeper sense Jesus was handed over to His Father's will and eternal purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
- Constable: Luke sets Jesus' innocence against Barabbas' guilt. He counts four declarations of innocence by Pilate; Pett counts three. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-23.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/luke-23.html

**v. 26: views differ on whether Simon became a believer**
- Jesus was too weak from the scourging to carry the cross. Cyrene was in North Africa. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23
- **Likely a believer:**
  - Guzik thinks Simon probably became a disciple and his sons became church leaders (Mark 15:21; Romans 16:13). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-23/
  - The Pulpit Commentary agrees and calls Simon a probable Passover pilgrim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/23-26.htm
  - MacArthur says Simon becomes a believer. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-284/characters-on-the-road-to-the-cross-part-2
- **Unknown:** The NET note is more cautious: Nothing more is known about this Simon. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23

**v. 27**
- Utley: the crowd was probably pilgrims just waking up to what had happened. The women were women of Jerusalem, not Jesus' Galilean followers. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-23
- Spurgeon also says these were Jerusalem women, not the Galilean disciples. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/wherefore-should-i-weep/

**v. 28: views differ on whether Jesus was rebuking the women**
- **Shared ground:** Jesus is warning of the coming destruction of Jerusalem.
  - Barnes refers it to the Roman desolation of the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-28.html
  - NET: the title "Daughters of Jerusalem" makes the women representatives of the nation. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Luk&chapter=23
  - MacArthur also reads the phrase as standing for the nation. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-284/characters-on-the-road-to-the-cross-part-2
- **Calvin (Reformed):** not a simple rebuke. Jesus is warning that His death is not the end, but the beginning, of evils to Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-28.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** strongly rejects the idea that the women were being scolded. Their tears were right, but they should weep more for the sin that made His death necessary, and for the punishment it would bring. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/23-28.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** comforts believers who cannot weep over the Passion; he says no one can share in Christ's atoning sufferings. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/luke/23-28.html
- **Matthew Henry:** their grief was natural ("worldly") sorrow, which Jesus redirected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/23-28.html
- **Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary:** this is the first recorded time Jesus speaks after leaving Pilate, and it shows His selflessness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/23-28.htm
- **Kevin DeYoung (TGC):** what looks like insensitivity is not the absence of love, but the deepest expression of it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/kevin-deyoung/do-not-weep-for-jesus/
- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** mentions speculation that "Daughters of Jerusalem" was the name of an organised group of women. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/crucifixion-part-1-luke
